This is the sixth time this project's narrow instrument has reported the page as worse than the page is, and the third time its error has been an under-count of a person, and a Volume 10 outline that inherits this floor must state Volume 09's answer as three of five and must not print two.**

OPEN, ADDED BY THIS PHASE AND CORRECTED BY THE PHASE THAT READ IT BACK, AND WHAT IT IS A FINDING ABOUT IS NOW THIS ITEM AND NOT THE CLOSE RECORD.** It was first printed as a record that contradicted itself, on the ground that the close's list of twenty pairs contains **0418↔0422** and that Chapters 0418 and 0422 are both inside the batch 0411 to 0420. **The batch arithmetic is false and it is the whole of the claim: Chapter 0418 is inside the batch 0411 to 0420 and Chapter 0422 is inside the batch 0421 to 0430, the pair crosses a boundary, and the close record's sentence is right where it stands.** Each of the five ranges was read out of its own batch prompt — 0401 to 0410, 0411 to 0420, 0421 to 0430, 0431 to 0440, 0441 to 0450 — and the close's twenty pairs were sorted against them one at a time: **all twenty cross a batch boundary, and the per-batch row of 0, 0, 0, 0 and 1 stands exactly as printed.** The `1` is the refrain at **0449↔0450**, both chapters inside the batch 0441 to 0450, and the close's own table names it in the row for the last ten against itself as *20w, 0449↔0450*; **that pair is not one of the twenty, because the twenty are prose and the refrain is formula, and the longer run 0449 and 0450 share is a date line and is excluded by the prose classification, which is why the row's pair is printed at twenty words and not at the row's largest.** Two pairs were offered in place of the wrong one and both are wrong in the same way — **0401↔0413 crosses, because 0413 is inside 0411 to 0420, and 0449↔0450 is not on the list of twenty at all** — and the correct set is none of them: there is no pair inside one batch among the twenty, and there was never a contradiction. **Nothing about the run is disturbed, because the correction is about the two chapter numbers and not about the run: it is forty-five words whitespace-tokenised and forty-four punctuation-stripped as first printed, it is not a date line, it is the identical sentence in both files — *said once that she would not say a second thing in that room and she has not, and she said nothing now, and there is no form anywhere in this empire for a clerk to be recorded as the one who did not speak* — and its tail is not any of the empire-formula's enumerated clause variants, so a list holding only those variants cannot classify it as formula, and none of that bears on batch membership, because the two chapters are not in one batch.**

**What is left standing is the standing the close handed on, and it is untouched, and the twenty pairs crossing every boundary is now the whole of its support instead of a defect in it: run the re-print instrument over the volume and not over the batch, every time, and the volume is fifty chapters and a batch is ten.** A writer who believed the withdrawn row would have run a per-batch check and reported it clean, which is the failure the standing was written to stop, **and a writer who believed this item would have gone looking for a second false figure among the close's instruments and found none, and item 64 and item 76 and this item are not one defect in three shapes but one correct standing and two wrong readings of it.**

**And the standing this item adds, which is the only part of it that will still be true next volume: a batch boundary is arithmetic, and it is tested a pair at a time before any pair is called internal, and a chapter number falling inside a written batch range is not inside that batch where the range ends before it.** This is the class item 106 names, in a new shape and in the other direction: the records were not worse than this item said, they were better, **and a negative finding is the most expensive kind to assert without the arithmetic under it, because it tells the next phase that something is broken that is not broken, and the next phase inherits it first.**

# THE PRINCIPALS AT THE CLOSE OF VOLUME 05, CHAPTER 250, CONSOLIDATED

**Written by the run that took the volume-close phase, `workspace/volume-05/volume-close/PROMPT.md`. One entry per principal, and not five entries per principal. No principal's state above this line is altered and none is deleted, because the entries above are the per-movement record and this section is the position at Chapter 250. An owed debt, a refusal, and an unanswered question are part of an entry and none of them is dropped: a consolidation that loses one of them is worse than no consolidation.**

**THE FOUR DEBTS THIS VOLUME OPENED ON A PERSON, AND THEY ARE FLAGGED IN THEIR OWN ENTRIES BELOW AND ARE NOT LOST ANYWHERE. One, Halla Wray: about nine men now know she is in a box, and there will not be another season in which she could ask one of the four who cannot read a paragraph, and nobody decided that and nothing was resolved. Two, the man of about thirty-four: he is a party and is findable by his own question, there is no form in this empire for asking a person whether they will mind being told something, and he has decided not to ask a second question. Three, the clerk of about fifty-three: she is the only person in this matter who is answerable in writing for a question, on her own motion, and there is no instrument anywhere that will let her be asked whether she meant it. Four, Tamsin Rook: the decision about whether she trusts his judgment, which is the volume's first debt, unmade, not on the page, and not made for her.** No romance has begun anywhere in this volume and none is implied, and the relationship lock held in all five movements: two instruments that were never merged, two boxes on a page ruled by hand that are not merged with either instrument, a rule used once and a correct non-use entered, an undertaking live and unretired and unamended and unexercised, and a fourth envelope untouched, unsent and unopened with the noun not used in the prose.

- **Marek Kest, thirty-eight.** **He chose it, and the choosing was the removal of the only person in this empire who could have refused him.** On the fourth day of the fourth week of the eighth month of the year after next, at about the fifth hour of the morning, he filled the twelfth line of a book with no office on it — empty since the third week of the ninth month of the year after — read it back once and read it back again with the second reading slower, and then chose a labour he can be refused, and said out loud that this is a worse position than the other one and that he has known it since the third week of the fourth month of the year after next, when a woman of twenty asked him whether anybody could protect him. **A man who cannot be found cannot be made answerable, and a person who asks a question in a room is a party from that day on, and the whole of the cost of a fifth asking is the price of being findable, and he cannot pay it twice.** The day comes out of about forty-four pounds a year; there is no fund and no form anywhere in this empire for a fund; **the road was walked zero times across all fifty chapters of this volume and nobody was sent.** **He has torn up the only document he has ever had** — a sheet of clean paper nobody in this empire has ever issued him, kept about nine weeks in the drawer of his table — and gave the reason out loud, which is that a person with a clean sheet in a drawer in a rented room is a person waiting to be asked something and therefore a person with a document, and that about four years is how long anything about him can be found for. He has opened the door to his bread and said nothing to the step. He answered a man of about thirty-four on a landing about the cost of the choice, gave the price of the day, refused the cost of the choice in the same breath, said he had said it once and was not going to say it twice, said the man did not hear it, and said he was not going to pretend to him that he did. **He has no certification, has held none at any point in five volumes, and is never shown withdrawing one; his bar came off on the twelfth of the ninth month of last year on an application of one line which he wrote himself, and that is the canon sentence word for word wherever it is carried.** The line about two inches long on the inside of his left wrist reads nothing, decides nothing, imposes no tether, and does not know where the ford is. **Owed and unpaid:** a labour nobody can instruct and cannot pay and cannot thank; about four years of findability; a day of his own money; a missing half of a day of a man's memory and the day is not coming back and there is no form anywhere in this empire for a person to have a day back; a woman of about thirty-five with a day-book in a lodging house who came about nine miles twice and is findable and he is not, and he has had since the third week of the fourth month of the year after next to find a way round what she said and there is not one; and the second half of the reason for staying, which he still has not said and is not going to say in a doorway twice.

- **Tamsin Rook, twenty-four, a clerk at the fourth counter for two years, two boxes on a page ruled by hand in her own book with the same name in both.** **THE FOURTH DEBT THIS VOLUME OPENED ON A PERSON IS HERS AND IT IS THE VOLUME'S FIRST DEBT: the decision about whether she trusts his judgment is not made, is not made in a room, and is not on the page, and no batch of this volume moved it.** She said in the fourth movement that two pieces of evidence is not a decision and three is not either, and that she has said it in about nine other rooms in other words, and that she is not going to say it in this one because she has said it enough. **In the closing movement she said out loud that she has wanted to be asked every working day since about the seventh month of next year, that a person who is not asked has not been given a duty, and that she had known that since about the seventh month of next year and had never once known that it did not apply to her until about four minutes ago — which was the first time in two years that anybody had asked her one question at all.** She also said out loud that she has been carrying a fact about a person of seventeen since the fourth day of the fourth week of the seventh month of the year after next, that it is in nine mouths and in no book, and that she cannot do one single thing with it. She used the rule of the twelfth month of last year once, in writing with a date, and answered it in a room in words with a date — the second half no, the first half yes, on the day you have written — and refused to tell him which day, and said out loud in the closing movement that she has not been asked one question by anybody since the second day of the first week of the first month of the year after next. **The man who came up her stairs came in the last week of the ninth month of the year after, he is not one of the four, he said a price she quoted twice because he had not caught it the first time, he has not come back, and she says out loud that she does not know whether what he asked her counted and that she has got no book that says and that there is nobody she could ask without asking a person to look themselves up.** **Owed and unpaid:** the decision; a fourth box, if there is one, and she will not say; the undertaking of the fourth of the first month, live, unretired, unamended and unexercised; the fourth envelope, in a drawer with three others, unsent, unopened, and the noun is not used in the prose; the price of being a party, said out loud ten times and never once thanked, which she said in advance nobody would be, and which nobody has; and a fact about a girl of seventeen that she cannot do one single thing with.

- **Halla Wray, fifty-one, foreman of the Slade Cut for nine years, in a box since the first week of the seventh month of the year after, entered by a class, never asked.** **THE FIRST OF THE FOUR DEBTS THIS VOLUME OPENED ON A PERSON IS HERS.** She told about nine men, in a bay and not in a doorway, on the second day of the second week of the ninth month of the year after next, that she has been entered in a box by a class and has never been asked one thing about it — on purpose, and the reason she gives is that being the only person who can say out loud what an entry in a box does to a life is a door and she would like to be found. **About nine men know she is in a box and not one of them has said a word about it since. There will not be another season in which a foreman of fifty-one could ask one of the four who cannot read a paragraph a question, and nobody decided that and nothing was resolved.** She refused to say what the box was for until a man of about thirty-four asked her, in a bay, in about nine men, on the fourth day of the fourth week of the eleventh month of the year after next, **what the word *representative* means**, and she answered: the form was not asking her whether she would represent anybody, it was asking who she represents, and there is a column for the answer and there is no column for a refusal, and that is why a no she said out loud in a room with the day on it did not work. Not because a clerk did anything wrong. Because there was nowhere to put it. She said out loud that what the man had just done had not changed one word of the position of the four and was never going to. She said out loud in the same batch that she has three bad reasons for not asking the reader of seventeen and no good one, and is not going to be told a fourth by anybody in that room who is not one of the four, and that is an admission and not a reason. **Her three standing decisions all hold and none was re-argued or re-staged: that she is not going to make herself easier to ask, that she is going to stop being glad of a thing nobody can check, and that she does not know the right reason about the reader of seventeen.** She has read a bay with her ears since she was forty-two and there is not one form anywhere in this empire that pays a woman for knowing where a man is standing, and she has never once told one of the four and is not going to. She walked up four hundred yards to a book-keeper's door and said one true thing to a person and not to a bay, and the chapter flags the cost on the page. **Owed and unpaid:** about four people in a bay who cannot read a paragraph and have never been asked anything; the half of a second sentence she has owed since the third month of the year after, which is unasked for and unasked about and cannot be got back, and the seventh month's arrangement is unbroken; about four hundred yards of ditch and a scour that were on nobody's list and are now on one with no figure against them; and the box, which has not got her out and is not going to.

- **Rennick Adley, thirty-eight, book-keeper of the Slade Cut Company, who has kept the Company's books since the second month of next year.** **His wages are held against a roof he put there on purpose and the document he made on purpose is the thing standing between himself and a wage he is owed.** He is not on the list of works and has never been on it, because a list of works is a list of works and a book-keeper does not do works, and he built that column with no names in it in the second month of next year **because a name in a column is a thing a person can be served at**, and a list of forty-one names goes into a company book about four hundred and thirty miles down this river in nine hands over about sixty years, and the newest hand in that book is his. The Company's whole money is four shillings a year and all of it is the rent of a hired stone store, taken out four times a year at a shilling a quarter, entered by him in one line in the second month of next year and read back twice. **The days he spends on the numbers of other people are not paid and cannot be, and he found that out at about the fourth hour of the sixth month of the year after next, and nobody ever told him, and a foreman of fifty-one on his own bank has known since the sixth year of a guild's blank list.** He read a man's own paper to him in a yard twice with a mark in chalk on a wall at the height of the third link of a chain, on a wall nobody looks at, and **the chain is on the man and the cross means nothing and is nobody's, and the reason it is there is that in about four years a person with a copy of the right page could put the cross and the wall and the yard together and ask a question about them and he would be the only person who could answer it.** He was offered the chance to enter a decision on his own account and refused to write it down. He read about nineteen reasons out of a column in a bay and did not stop a man standing up with his own. He has worked out, after about four days, that the reason he could not account for the entry about the reader of seventeen is structural: a reason under an entry about a person needs a day, a day about a person needs a name, and there is no name in that column. **He is one of about four people in this matter who cannot be asked anything and he is not one of the four who cannot read a paragraph, and the two are not the same and a chapter that merges them breaks the matter.** **Owed and unpaid:** his own wage; the reason for the entry with no reason under it, which he has now and has not written down; the half of a sentence a foreman owes him, which he has said he wants and is not going to ask for; and the about nine hundred and forty names in a company book that has four hundred dead people in it, which is why he is not going to put two words in it.

- **Nell Kest, twenty, a dye-house worker, sixteen books, a furnace town about four hundred and thirty miles up this river.** **She has decided to go and tell four women that she is not paid, and she has told one, and nobody has thanked her and there is not going to be a form for it.** The decision falls in the fourth week of the ninth month of the year after next. She refused money from a woman of about thirty who has some — **the first time in about three years — and gave the reason out loud, which is that if she takes it then she is a trade and a trade can be told what to do, and the woman cannot be told what to do, and that is the only thing she has got.** The woman said *then you will not have it when I am gone*, and she answered that a person who keeps another person's numbers for nothing is keeping them for the four years and not for the person, and that she chose the four years on purpose out of sixteen books and not out of one. Fifteen of the sixteen are other people's, none has an office on it, one has her own name at the head of it, and **if somebody came up those stairs with a sheet and a seal she could not show a soul the fourth of them.** Her wage has been held since the second week of the third month of the year after by a man who cannot say what it is held against, and the money for nineteen days is in a weigh-house ledger with her wage in it and not her name under it. A foreman off a dye end has come up two stairs four times, said the same three things each time, and held a wage-day notice in a coat without sending it; she has told him what to do instead — write it, keep it, do not send it — and has said the reason is one she made up in about four seconds and would not be thanked for. She is not going up the river this season and has not said she is never going to, and she is the only person who knows there is a difference between the two. **Owed and unpaid:** three of the four women untold and no fund for the telling; the sixteenth book; a wage held since the second week of the third month of the year after; a room where nobody is to be told; and a letter of hers to a man of about thirty-eight that he has not answered and is not going to be able to.

- **The man of about thirty-four with a trade, a house with a door on it and a wife, and a bedroom at the back of it, who asked the fifth question.** **THE SECOND OF THE FOUR DEBTS THIS VOLUME OPENED ON A PERSON IS HIS.** He is not a clerk and not a foreman and not a man of thirty-eight and nobody sent him, and he is the sixth person in the manuscript to ask a question on purpose and the second to do it for no reason a foreman gave him. He asked, on the fourth day of the fourth week of the eleventh month of the year after next, in a bay, in about nine men, **what the word *representative* means**, and she answered. **He is now a party and is findable by his own question, and there is no form anywhere in this empire for asking a person whether they will mind being told something.** He told his wife on purpose six weeks before he went, without asking her first, and said out loud that he could have asked and did not, because if he had asked she would have said no or said yes and been frightened, and both of those would have been him arranging the room. He wrote the count on the back of his own hand in a pencil that was nearly blunt and it was gone in about four weeks, and he wrote the four of them on the inside of his own hat, **which is the only place any of them has ever been.** He asked a man of about fifty-five with a chain, in a yard, whether anybody had ever asked a person out loud what a word on a form means, and was told them in the wrong order on purpose with a date against each, and was told that a list of four of them is a list, and a list has a heading, and about nine people in that city could write either heading and both would be true and neither would be any use. He said out loud to the foreman who had answered him that he did not know how to be a person who has asked, and she told him what it costs and he heard it. **At the end of the volume he decided he will not do it again, and gave the reason himself, and the reason is the volume's own finding about its own climax: a person who does a thing twice has made a practice, and a practice grows a heading over it on its own without anybody deciding anything, and a heading is how a person becomes a company.** He is going back to being a man on a list of works four times a season with a fair hand on somebody else's page. **Owed and unpaid:** findability he did not choose and did not ask his wife about; a question answered in a bay by a person who is in a box, which he cannot un-hear and cannot return; and the whole of the rest of the four who cannot read a paragraph, which his asking did not touch and which he was told out loud would not be touched.

- **The clerk of about fifty-three in the office of a seat, who is on the page by name in four chapters of this volume as Orla Denning and is not named in the chapter where she entered the question.** **THE THIRD OF THE FOUR DEBTS THIS VOLUME OPENED ON A PERSON IS HERS.** Nineteen years of eleven minute books on a shelf in a room with a window about two feet wide and a pane out of it, about four thousand entries in those books and no name in any one of them, and that is not carelessness, it is the only shape a minute book has got. Not a lawyer, not a party, not a judge, and **she is the only person in this matter who cannot be examined and the only one who is paid nothing, and those are the same reason and nobody has ever put them together.** She said out loud in a shed in the fifth month of the year after next, to a foreman's face, **that a seat is a thing in a room without being a person**, and a clerk who says a thing like that in a room writes it down, and it is in one of the eleven books in her own hand with the day on it. She entered a date four years off for a room in which a person described and not named, about sixty-three, is to be asked whether there is more of her than nine lines, and she did not know what she was entering and entered what she was given and said so in the room and wrote that down, and said that a clerk of nineteen years who says afterwards that she did not know is a clerk of nineteen years who was asked. She is the clerk whose own hand is at the foot of a printed return that asks for the person, institution or thing engaged in a matter and that has a person of twenty in it, four hundred and thirty miles from that desk, entered correctly in the ordinary way by a person who was not asked, and her own name is at the foot of that sheet and it is the second thing in this matter with her hand at the foot of it and the first one she did not choose. She took that file out of the ordinary course, wrote a second line under the box, and had it read out loud on the stairs, both lines, and said out loud that a form does not get asked anything by a man with a tray and a woman does and there is not going to be a post for it. She worked out in about four days that **a heading is how a person becomes a company, and a company is a thing this empire can hold wages against and give letters to and take to law, and a man who is a person is a thing it can only send papers to**, and said it out loud in a bay four hundred and thirty miles away on the same day, and **the two of them have never met and there is no instrument in this empire that would put them in a room.** She went and looked for about two days, on her own time, unpaid, for a procedure for un-filling a box, and there is not one, and about nine hundred entries in nineteen years did not produce it. **On her own motion, at nobody's request, she entered a question in the second of eleven minute books in her own hand with the day on it and her own name at the foot of it: whether an entry made in a box by a class may be un-filled, and if it may not by whom it is to remain, and if it may on whose application, to whom that application is to be addressed, and by what hand it is to be received. It is the only new instrument in this matter in fifty chapters. She is now the only person in this matter who is answerable in writing for a question, and there is no instrument anywhere in this empire that will let her be asked whether she meant it.** **Owed and unpaid:** the answer to the question she entered, which nobody has to give her; the second line under a box on a file head in a corridor, which is worth fourpence of ink and which she has to be able to explain in about four years; a name she knows and has not said out loud in her own office and is not going to; a return that is a roll of households being asked for a person and getting one; and the refusal she entered with a reason so that the not-answering is on the record, and the reason, which is that the only document that would bear on it is a document that cannot be produced by anybody.

- **Marn Ottery, thirty-four, eleven years at the fourth counter, about four hundred bought and unfilled blanks in a box under it.** **She asked a colleague one question out loud for the first time in eleven years, and it was not a question about a word on a form, and she said the shape of it out loud before she asked it** — that a board is not a form and a line of writing on a board is not a word on a form — and that she had thought about it for about four days and was going to ask it anyway and wanted it noticed that she thought about it. She told a woman of about forty who came up the stairs for a copy and asked about a name and not about the paper, **that a name in a column is a thing a person can be served at**, which she has said at that counter about four hundred times to rooms and once to a person, and she put the coin back on the counter rather than taking it, which is not a thing a clerk does. She said out loud what the box is for, to a colleague, for the first time in eleven years: **a blank is the only piece of paper in this empire that cannot be held against anybody, and a Table is the only place where a person can come up, ask a question, and walk away with a piece of paper that says they asked it, and that is the nearest thing to a post that anybody has ever built, and it is not a post and it will not become one, and if it became one it would stop on the day the first person with a form wanted it to.** She has kept the blanks for eleven years with no form for it and is not going to stop. **Owed and unpaid:** the answer to a question about a line of writing on a fee board that nobody can answer; the fourth thing on that board that she and two other clerks cannot account for; about four hundred blanks' worth of nothing; a counter open from the second hour to the sixth; and a thing she wanted for herself in this matter for two years and did not have on purpose.

- **The foreman off a dye end, about forty, a furnace town about four hundred and thirty miles up this river, one of about four people in this matter who cannot be asked, holding a wage-day notice in a coat.** **He is the only person in that city who can pick up or put down the whole of a woman's money and he has said out loud that he cannot say what a wage is held against, and he has said it four times to men who were working and once to a boy of about nine with a slate, and the boy is the fifth.** He worked it out in a rented room in a city four hundred and thirty miles down this river that he is one of about four people in this matter who cannot be asked, and he was told it by somebody and has said so. **On the second day of the first week of the eleventh month of the year after next he said the volume's own question out loud in his own mouth, four times over about half an hour to about nine men in a dye end: if that office was meant to be temporary, then somebody changed it into an inheritable one, and I would like to know who, and I have asked it in a shed in a different city in the fifth month of the year after next and nobody answered, and I am asking it again in my own mouth and nobody is going to answer it here either.** He did it on purpose and said the cost out loud, and a man of about fifty-five with a chain's reason came back at him: **a man who cannot read a paragraph is the only person in this empire you can say anything to and have it not come back.** A man of about forty says there was nobody to change; a man of about forty-four says it has not been improved on in about four weeks; a man of about twenty-six says the question is about four hundred and thirty miles away and not about a vat. **A boy of about nine wrote it on a slate with no name on it, and there is not one form anywhere in this empire that will take a slate off a boy, and the foreman said out loud that if there were one she would not fill it in, and that was the first thing she had said that year that was about herself.** He said out loud that he is not going to be the man who goes up that road and stands in that bay when the man of about thirty-four asks his question, because that would turn a thing a person did on purpose into a thing two people did. **He left the other half of the question alone on purpose and the only person who will ever know that he knew there was one is a man of about twenty-six.** The notice is still in the coat and he is not going to tell anybody, and the document is the only one in this matter that could be held to him. **Owed and unpaid:** the volume's own question, in five mouths and in no book at all; a wage he cannot say what it is held against; a list of works he held twice for nothing in forty years; a boy with a slate nobody has thanked; and a day-book of his own that is not there and has not been there for about nine years and that he has thought about about four times.

- **Bess Tarrant, sixty-three, of this city, and the only person in this matter who has chosen findability on purpose and for no procedural reason.** She put a man's name into a letter in the fourth week of the third month of the year after next and asked in her own hand that it not be written down. **Saying a name in a street is not the same as being found, and that has not changed in this volume, and she chose it anyway, three times, to nobody, and it has never once worked in her favour.** A day in a minute book has her name at the foot of it and she has decided not to find out about it, **and her only protection is that in about four years she will be sixty-seven and will be able to say she did not know.** She is unfindable for nine years and no other span. **Owed and unpaid:** the date four years off, unlooked into, unprinted, and not going to be looked into by her; and a surname that is not a door and has never been one and bought the person who received her hand nothing.

- **Ivet Sarn, thirty-eight, a clerk at a window, nine years at it, and the fifth instance of a thing two courts have now said four times.** **Her fourth column is still empty and still a waste and still has no heading over it, and the door a couple of inches open halfway along her corridor is still neither shut nor entered.** She refused a seventh column in a form, with a reason and no why, and distinguished a refusal from a declination to answer, because a refusal in one form on three days is a document and a declination would leave it open for somebody to ask the same question in about four years in a different room. She gave the court what it could instead: a sixth ruled space at the bottom of every page of that register, which has never had a heading over it and which about two hundred and forty people in that district have never known is there, and one line in her own hand with a day on it. She identified a living man's hand by comparison on a delivery stub in about nine minutes and is a party and is therefore told everything. **Two of the four places that file is in are a back room off a corridor she has walked every working day for nine years and has never been inside, and a line in a margin in a hand that is not his, written by a provincial archivist on the ordinary round who gave it away for nothing, is not thanked, and does not know that her hand is in a file four hundred and thirty miles from her own office.** **Owed and unpaid:** the file of the sixth year, shut between two others; an undertaking that is hers in a stranger's hand and has been used four times without her; the question of who wrote thirty-one letters that she entered herself as not knowing; the numbers on her wall, which are unchanged and still true and are not restated; and a witness status that can be restored, which she will not be the one to ask for.

- **And the unnamed figures this volume is careful with, all of them still unnamed and all of them exactly where they were.** **About four people in a bay who cannot read a paragraph**, of whom one is a man of about fifty-five with a chain who held the four in his head and had nothing written and said out loud that he is the only person on that bank that findability does not work on, that he had known it for about four years, that he had never once used it, and that he wanted it said that he knew what he was doing — **and who says out loud that he is not one of the four, has not been asked one thing in nine years, and that writing him down as one of them would be a way for a list of four to go wrong.** A man of about thirty from a second gang, findable by his own reason since the fourth day of the fourth week of the seventh month, who has decided not to have it taken back and whose decision was refused in writing. A man of about thirty with fourpence in his hand who did not spend it and has a wife. A man of about forty-four who has not slept since the first time a question was said in his end and has told his wife nothing. A man of about thirty-four who came four miles in the rain and could not finish a question, and who did not come back. A woman of about thirty-five who keeps a day-book in a lodging house, who came about nine miles twice and was not let in and wrote none of it down. A man of about thirty who is findable and not going to be asked about a rate twice. A woman of about thirty who has money and offered some of it. **A boy of about nine with a slate, now with two slates in about four years, the second one with the office question on it and no name on it, and nobody has thanked him and nobody ever has.** **And a reader of seventeen, on the page nine times across this volume, unnamed, not the point of view, not the person who is asked anything, not spoken to about the season, not thanked, not sent for and not going to be.** She is on a written engagement at forty-five pence a day and four days a week, and the reader's engagement is not printed in this volume and no elapsed period is computed from it. **Three reasons are spent and are not to be restated: a foreman's decision not to tell her she is the one person who could read the hold, a book-keeper's entry with no reason under it, and a man of about fifty-five's reason that a thing a person does for money is a thing somebody can write down.** A fourth reason is new and is a working man's and is not about being paid: she would say yes, and there is nothing in this empire she can do about being asked in a room, and in about four years there will be a person who can say that a girl of seventeen stood in a bay and read a hold out loud, and there is no form that requires a person to say it and no form that says she may refuse to have said it. **A foreman of fifty-one has said out loud that she has three bad reasons and no good one and is not going to be told a fourth by anybody who is not one of the four. Nobody was thanked anywhere in this volume, because there is not one form anywhere in this empire that requires it, and this was the last season in which anybody on that bank could ask her something and be answered for nothing.**

# WHAT THE VOLUME 07 OUTLINE DOES TO EACH PRINCIPAL, ADDED BENEATH THE CONSOLIDATED ROSTER AND NOT INSTEAD OF IT

*Appended by the run that took `workspace/volume-07/volume-07-outline/PROMPT.md`, the volume-outline phase, which writes no prose and changes no page. **The consolidated one-entry-per-principal position at Chapter 300 is the section above this one and is not replaced by a second set and is not restated here: this section adds only what `outline/volume-07.md` changes, and names the movement each change belongs to, and an owed debt, a refusal and an unanswered question are part of every entry and none of them is dropped, because a consolidation that loses one of them is worse than no consolidation.** Nothing here is resolved. Nobody is thanked. Nobody is sent. The four hundred and thirty miles is walked zero times. New named figures the outline plans: none, and that is eleven consecutive batches.*

**The man of about thirty-four with a fair hand — the volume's climax is his, and it is a not-doing.** The outline gives him a third journey of nine miles in **Movement 5, Chapters 0346 to 0348**, and on that journey he has the eighth question ready and **does not ask it**, and he says out loud, in a room, why he is not going to, and the reason is about nine sentences and it is the volume's finding. **He comes back and he tells nobody what was said in that room, and the bill for being findable is still not his, and his wife is not thanked, has not been thanked, did not ask him how it went, and said out loud that she is not going to.** Owed and unpaid and not paid in this volume: the second asking he swore in a doorway he would not do and did; the form in this empire for asking a person whether they will mind being told something, which does not exist; the bill for findability, which is not his; and the thing nobody thanked him for. **Movement 1 is his ordinary week and it is a week in which he asks nothing.**

**Tamsin Rook, the clerk of twenty-four at the fourth counter — and the check that names her is three lines long and is in the outline.** Chapter 0261 names her at that counter and Chapter 0265 has her at the other end of it saying she has been in that room two years, and the Volume 05 roster above gives her as twenty-four at that counter for two years: **the person the plan calls Tamsin and the clerk of twenty-four at the fourth counter are one person and are not a merge, and no Volume 07 card may treat them as two.** The outline gives her **Movements 1 and 2 at the counter, and then nothing.** **She is asked nothing in this volume and that is entered as a choice and not as a fault, and the sixth reason her undertaking of the fourth of the first month is unexercised is not a variation of the first five: nobody asked her and this volume did not ask her either.** What changes is that she works out, in a room of her own, that the line she put in her own book about a woman eleven years at the other end of that counter is a window and not a wall, and that **there is not one form anywhere in this empire for taking a line out of a book of your own.** Owed and unpaid: the answer to the question she was asked and did not give; **the decision about whether she trusts his judgment, unmade, not on the page, and not made in a room and not made for her**; a fourth box, if there is one, which she will not say; the undertaking, live, unretired, unamended, unexercised; the fourth thing in her drawer, untouched, unsent, unopened; the price of being a party said out loud ten times and never once thanked; and a fact about a person of seventeen that is in nine mouths and in no book and that she can do not one single thing with. **No romance begins and none is implied.**

**Marek Kest, thirty-eight — the volume's change is a refusal and a non-use, and the power obligation is not paid twice.** **Movement 1 gives him a rented room, about four feet of a wall nobody uses, and a decision not to attempt the reading: two attempts have already taken two separate days of his mother's own history out of him, he can no longer remember whether he left a room or stood in a doorway, and the third one is not a thing he is going to spend on a man at a rail, and he gives the reason out loud.** **Movement 4 gives him a bay, about nine men in it, and one thing said out loud: he is not going up the stair at the top of it, because going up it would put Tamsin Rook in the room, since two instruments require that and they are not one instrument, and she has been the price of a party out loud ten times and has not been thanked once, and he is not going to do it an eleventh time — and she is not told that he said it.** He is not in the climax room and is not sent and does not go. **He does not exercise Stage 2, a correct non-use is entered as one, he does not attempt the reading, he does not reach a stage, and the mark is a symptom and reads nothing and decides nothing and does not know where the ford is, and the wage is the price.** Owed and unpaid: the labour he chose is not re-decided and is not paid again; nobody thanked him for a thing he did not do and there is not one form anywhere in this empire that requires a person to be thanked for not doing a thing; and the reason he is the most dangerous person in this matter is that nobody in it can tell him to stop.

**The man of about sixty-one who signs at the foot of every sheet — the volume's address, and he is not in the roster above and is added here because the volume turns on him.** He has been the second hand since he was forty-two, signs about nine hundred sheets a year out of one building off the old river road, **cannot read a paragraph**, and has come about nine miles twice in nineteen years, both times in a season, both times on a tell from a carrier in a lane, and **there is no form in this empire for asking a man of sixty-one to walk nine miles so that a clerk can put a hand on the foot of a sheet.** About nine of about nine hundred a year have not been what the person above him wrote and he signed them, and he would want about four minutes to say no to about half and yes to the rest, and **there is nobody to ask.** **Movement 3 has him come a third time and say the same true thing standing up in about nine minutes, and Movement 5 has him in the climax room and asked nothing.** Owed and unpaid: about four minutes; about nine sheets; the reason nobody has asked, which is that he would tell the truth; and the two halves of the arrangement, which are the same arrangement and which he has never put in one sentence. **He is not one of the four men in a bay and is never in a list with them, and a chapter that puts him there has invented a fifth and has also turned four people into a method.**

**The clerk of about fifty-three in the office of a seat — she is asked nothing in this volume and that is the volume's rule working.** **Movement 3 has her in the room with him and not asking, and Movement 5 has her in the room with the eighth question ready and not being asked, and in both she writes none of it down and says out loud why: a minute with an answer in it is an order and a clerk of that office has not entered one in nineteen years and there is no form that lets her.** **She is not asked a second time by anybody and the season does not change that.** Owed and unpaid: the answer to a question in her own book, a quarter of which was given out loud in a room in the second month of the year after the year after next and went nowhere; the fact that she is the only person in this matter answerable in writing for a question and is paid nothing; and about four thousand entries in eleven books with no name in any one of them, which is not carelessness and is the only shape a minute book has got.

**Halla Wray, fifty-one, foreman of the Slade Cut — in a box, entered by a class, and the volume's finding is about her class without being about her.** **Movement 2 establishes that a question at a scale is a question about a class, and a class is a heading, and she is one: entered by one in the first week of the seventh month of the year after and never asked about it.** **Movement 4 gives the price of the class in people: about nine men know she is in a box, that is nine mouths and not a document, and the season has closed and nobody decided that and nothing was resolved, and there will not be another season in which a foreman of fifty-one could ask one of the four who cannot read a paragraph a question.** Owed and unpaid: the second sentence she owes, wanted by a book-keeper four hundred yards up that lane who has not asked and is not going to, and **the day he asks is the day she stops saying the half she has got, and nobody asks in this volume**; and the form that put her there has not been asked to be void by anybody.

**Rennick Adley, thirty-eight, book-keeper of the Slade Cut Company — his column is the volume's second movement's machine, and he is not rescued and not thanked.** **Movement 2 puts his column with no names in it, built in the second month of next year because a name in a column is a thing a person can be served at, beside a column headed *next review* with nothing in it and a correct sum in a third hand under a ruled line in a day-book four miles off, and the movement's finding is that a column with a heading over it is a machine and a column with no heading over it is a person.** Owed and unpaid: the second sentence; about nineteen days' money in a weigh-house ledger; the fourth thing on a fee board about four hundred yards away that he cannot account for; and a mark in chalk on a wall that is about four years from being anybody's evidence. **The outline does not give him the second sentence and the not-asking is still the volume's finding reached by a different man in a different place and said to nobody.**

**Nell Kest, twenty, a dye-house worker, sixteen books — four hundred and thirty miles up this river, and this volume does not move her and does not thank her.** **Movement 1 has her in the counting room with three women still untold and no fund for the telling, and the practice's other end, and nobody in the building she works in knows that a man nine miles off a building off the old river road has done a thing on purpose twice.** Owed and unpaid: three of the four women untold; the sixteenth book; a wage held since the second week of the third month of the year after by a man who cannot say what it is held against; and a foreman in a coat with a notice in it who has said out loud that the day he wants it to exist he will send it. **She is not going up the river this season and has not said she is never going to, and nobody has thanked her and there is not going to be a form for it.**

**Marn Ottery, thirty-four, a clerk at the fourth counter, eleven years, about four hundred bought and unfilled blanks in a box under it — the argument is spent and the outline does not spend it again.** **The box is not a post, it has no form for keeping it, and it has been refused twice in a room in about four minutes, and this volume adds no third refusal and no third asking and the box goes back under the counter where it goes.** **Movement 2 is hers: she is the person at the top of the stair who says out loud what a question has to be about to be asked of about nine hundred rooms, and the reason it works is that a border household is not a person, and the counterpart, that a person is the one thing a class cannot be asked about.** Owed and unpaid: the answer to a question about a line of writing on a fee board that nobody can answer; the fourth thing on that board that she and two other clerks cannot account for; about four hundred blanks' worth of nothing; and a thing she wanted for herself in this matter for two years and did not have on purpose. **She is not thanked and does not expect it and this volume does not thank her.**

**The foreman off a dye end, about forty — he is the other end of the practice's geography and this volume does not put him in a room with anybody.** **Movement 1 has his end of the river, his stove, his eleven houses off a dyers' lane and a boy of about nine with two slates, the second with the office question on it and no name on it, and the fact that he said the volume's own question out loud four times in about half an hour to about nine men and a man of about fifty-five with a chain came back at him.** Owed and unpaid: who changed a temporary office into an inheritable one; a wage held with no name against it; a notice in a coat that he has said out loud he will send on a day he chooses; and a boy nobody has thanked.

**The woman of about twenty-six at the end of the cold passage — the volume gives her the one scene it is built to pay and she does not pay it.** **Movement 5, Chapters 0341 to 0345: she comes about four hundred yards up that passage to the top of a stair with a figure she has carried in her head for about four years, and she does not give it, and the reason is out loud, and the reason is that a number that has never been in a book is the only number nobody can take off a person, and the day it is in a book it is a column, and a column wants a heading, and a heading over that figure is a heading over about nine hundred rooms, and then a corridor a person has stood at the end of for about four years stops being the end of anything. Nobody asks her what she came for. She goes back down and does not say by how much the figure has gone up.** Owed and unpaid: the figure she will not give and will not hand on; three questions for a man of about sixty-one that she will not ask; and the third word on the slate, which exists and has no name on it. **The coming is findable and there is no form anywhere that would let anybody ask her about it and she was not thanked and nobody thanked her.**

**The others, and every debt this volume leaves standing on them, and nothing here is resolved.** **About four men in a bay who cannot read a paragraph, unnamed, still never asked one question about a number, in any chapter of fifty and in none of this volume's fifty, and a chapter that asks them breaks the volume.** The man of about fifty-five with a chain who says out loud that he is not one of the four and that writing him down as one of them would be a way for a list of four to go wrong, and who has known for about four years that findability does not work on him and has never once used it, **and the volume's fourth rule is that he is not a method.** The reader of seventeen at the back of that bay on a written engagement, unnamed, unspoken to, unthanked, unsent for, not going to start. The girl of seventeen in the same bay, in the same condition, and a chapter that thanks her breaks the volume. A man of about thirty from the second gang, findable and not going to be asked about a rate twice. A man of about thirty with fourpence in his hand who did not spend it and has a wife. A man of about forty-four who has not slept since the first time a question was said in his end. A man of about thirty-four who came four miles in the rain and could not finish a question and did not come back. A woman of about thirty-five with a day-book in a lodging house who came about nine miles twice, was not let in, and wrote none of it down. A woman of about thirty who has money and offered some of it. A boy of about nine with two slates and no name on either. **And two boxes that stay shut, a guarantee that stands unanswered with about sixty children inside it, and a bill at nineteen pounds three and fourpence that nobody is liable for.**
